summary.text: The formal statement reverses the intended Legendre symbol, using \((7/p)\) in place of \((p/7)\); at \(p=11\), quadratic reciprocity gives \((7/11)=-1\). A direct finite evaluation gives the weighted sum as \(227535863206839\equiv44\pmod{121}\), whereas the asserted right-hand side is \(11(21(-1)+16)=-55\equiv66\pmod{121}\), so the congruence fails.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
a(n)=\sum_{j=0}^{n}\binom nj^2\binom{n-j}{j}^2(-16)^j
\]
and let
\[
W(p)=\sum_{k=0}^{p-1}(42k+37)(-1)^k a(k).
\]

There is an essential notational point concerning the assertion being disproved. The accepted formal statement defines its auxiliary symbol at a prime \(p\) to be the Legendre symbol
\[
\left(\frac{7}{p}\right),
\]
so its asserted congruence is
\[
W(p)\equiv p\left(21\left(\frac{7}{p}\right)+16\right)\pmod{p^2}.
\tag{1}
\]
This reverses the numerator and denominator in the canonical conjecture, which has \(\left(\frac{p}{7}\right)\). We now disprove (1) by taking \(p=11\).

First, \(11\) is prime and \(11\ne7\), so it satisfies all the hypotheses of (1). We evaluate the Legendre symbol on its right-hand side. The nonzero quadratic residues modulo \(11\) are
\[
1^2\equiv1,\quad 2^2\equiv4,\quad 3^2\equiv9,\quad
4^2\equiv5,\quad 5^2\equiv3\pmod {11};
\]
the remaining nonzero squares repeat these residues. Thus the set of nonzero quadratic residues modulo \(11\) is
\[
\{1,3,4,5,9\}.
\]
Since \(7\) is not in this set, it is a quadratic nonresidue modulo \(11\), and hence
\[
\left(\frac{7}{11}\right)=-1.
\tag{2}
\]

It remains to evaluate \(W(11)\). This is a finite calculation directly from the defining binomial sum. In calculating \(a(n)\), terms with \(j>n-j\) vanish because then \(\binom{n-j}{j}=0\). The nonzero inner summands
\[
\binom nj^2\binom{n-j}{j}^2(-16)^j
\]
for \(0\le n\le10\), followed by their sums, are as follows:
\[
\begin{array}{c|l|r}
n&\text{nonzero inner summands, in increasing order of }j&a(n)\\ \hline
0&1&1\\
1&1&1\\
2&1,-64&-63\\
3&1,-576&-575\\
4&1,-2304,9216&6913\\
5&1,-6400,230400&224001\\
6&1,-14400,2073600,-1638400&420801\\
7&1,-28224,11289600,-80281600&-69020223\\
8&1,-50176,45158400,-1284505600,321126400&-918270975\\
9&1,-82944,146313216,-11560550400,26011238400&14596918273\\
10&1,-129600,406425600,-72253440000,650280960000,-66588770304
&511845045697
\end{array}
\]
For example, every row is obtained simply by inserting the displayed value of \(n\) into the definition. For \(n=4\), the three nonzero terms are
\[
\binom40^2\binom40^2=1,
\]
\[
\binom41^2\binom31^2(-16)=16\cdot9\cdot(-16)=-2304,
\]
and
\[
\binom42^2\binom22^2(-16)^2=36\cdot1\cdot256=9216,
\]
whose sum is \(6913\); all the other rows are computed in exactly the same way.

We now multiply these values by their respective outer weights \((42k+37)(-1)^k\). This gives
\[
\begin{array}{c|r|r|r}
k&42k+37&a(k)&(42k+37)(-1)^k a(k)\\ \hline
0&37&1&37\\
1&79&1&-79\\
2&121&-63&-7623\\
3&163&-575&93725\\
4&205&6913&1417165\\
5&247&224001&-55328247\\
6&289&420801&121611489\\
7&331&-69020223&22845693813\\
8&373&-918270975&-342515073675\\
9&415&14596918273&-6057721083295\\
10&457&511845045697&233913185883529
\end{array}
\]
Adding the last column yields
\[
W(11)=227535863206839.
\tag{3}
\]
To reduce this number modulo \(11^2=121\), note that
\[
227535863206839=121\cdot1880461679395+44.
\]
Consequently,
\[
W(11)\equiv44\pmod{121}.
\tag{4}
\]

On the other hand, (2) makes the right-hand side asserted in (1) equal to
\[
11\left(21\left(\frac{7}{11}\right)+16\right)
=11(21(-1)+16)
=11(-5)
=-55.
\]
Modulo \(121\), this is
\[
-55\equiv66\pmod{121}.
\tag{5}
\]
The residues in (4) and (5) are distinct: \(44\ne66\). Equivalently, their difference is
\[
44-(-55)=99,
\]
which is not divisible by \(121\). Therefore
\[
W(11)\not\equiv11\left(21\left(\frac{7}{11}\right)+16\right)\pmod{121}.
\]
Thus the universally quantified assertion (1) is false, with \(p=11\) as a counterexample.

For completeness, this counterexample arises precisely from the reversal of the Legendre symbol and does not disprove the canonically stated congruence using \(\left(\frac{p}{7}\right)\). Indeed,
\[
\left(\frac{11}{7}\right)=\left(\frac47\right)=1
\]
because \(4\equiv2^2\pmod7\). The canonical right-hand side at \(p=11\) is therefore
\[
11(21\cdot1+16)=407\equiv44\pmod{121},
\]
which agrees with (4). The disproof is specifically of the accepted formal proposition, whose symbol is \(\left(\frac{7}{p}\right)\). The distinction is also explained by quadratic reciprocity: because both \(7\) and \(11\) are congruent to \(3\pmod4\),
\[
\left(\frac{7}{11}\right)=-\left(\frac{11}{7}\right).
\]
